claims.text: The formation and crystal-structure selection of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by competition between rapid kinetic quenching and thermally activated atomic diffusion.
Rapid heating and cooling provide insufficient time for atomic diffusion.
Insufficient diffusion time preserves or produces local composition fluctuations.
Local composition fluctuations trigger phase separation.
Local composition fluctuations cause elemental segregation.
Diffusion-limited rapid processing leads to uncontrolled or anomalous particle morphologies.
An extended intermediate-temperature dwell or slower cooling ramp increases the time available for atomic diffusion.
Greater diffusion time at intermediate temperatures increases atomic mobility and elemental redistribution.
Increased elemental redistribution homogenizes the nanoparticles.
Atomic homogenization favors formation of a uniform single-phase solid solution with the targeted crystal structure.
Rapid cooling kinetically traps nanoparticles in non-equilibrium phases or morphologies.
Slower cooling will produce more uniform single-phase nanoparticles than rapid cooling.
Slower cooling will reduce elemental segregation and phase separation relative to rapid cooling.
Slower cooling will improve control of particle morphology relative to rapid cooling.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles whose constituent elements have moderately disparate surface energies and diffusion barriers.
The intervention is effective only in a temperature window where diffusion is appreciable and thermal decomposition has not begun.
At extremely high or low temperatures, mechanisms other than diffusion-versus-quenching may govern structure selection.
The cooling-rate threshold and optimal temperature window vary with particle size, composition, and elemental properties.
